definition: Too ready to believe what you are told, even without good evidence.
example: Credulous readers shared the fake headline before checking whether any of it was true.
nuance: Credulous describes a person who believes too easily; credible describes a claim or source that deserves belief.
prompt: At a county fair, a stranger claims his tonic can make hair grow back overnight.
options: The credulous visitor bought three bottles without asking for any proof.
The salesman's credulous claim was backed by careful laboratory tests.
The credulous visitor demanded to see evidence and then walked away completely unconvinced.
The visitor stared in credulous disbelief at such an absurd promise.
reasons: Paying for an unlikely promise without demanding evidence shows a person who believes too easily.
This mixes it up with credible; a well-supported claim is believable, and claims are not the ones doing the believing.
Insisting on proof and staying doubtful is skepticism, the reverse of easy belief.
Disbelief calls for incredulous; the word without the prefix means believing, not doubting.

practice.prompt: A rumor spreads through a middle school that classes will be canceled for a month.
options: The rumor sounded so credulous that nobody bothered to question it.
Priya gave a credulous laugh, certain the whole story had been made up.
Being credulous, Mia packed away her books before anyone had confirmed the news.
Credulous as ever, Jonah phoned the front office to check whether the rumor was true.
reasons: A believable story is credible; the word in question describes people who believe, not stories.
Being sure a story is invented shows doubt, which is the opposite of what the word means.
Acting on an unverified rumor as though it were fact shows belief given too readily.
Checking a story before accepting it is caution, not easy belief.
